title: A Harbor for the Bridge
premise: In 1911, in the contested port city of Vellmark, apprentice clockmaker Lior Okafor is summoned to repair the observatory's master clock and discovers a hidden ledger inside its case — a record of every name the town's magistrates erased: the disappeared, the deported, the quietly murdered during the border wars. When the imperial army requisitions the town and seizes the observatory as a signals station, the ledger becomes the only proof of what happened, and the only thing standing between the victors' historians and a clean, bloodless official record. Lior, who has spent fifteen years surviving by knowing which silences keep people safe, must choose between that silence and testimony — aided by Captain Ilse Brandt, the occupying officer assigned to inventory the clockworks, who is beginning to doubt the army she serves. As armistice negotiations stall and the order comes to burn the archive, Lior and Ilse smuggle the ledger out through the harbor in the dead of night, at the cost of Ilse's commission and nearly Lior's life. The book ends with the ledger read aloud in the provisional assembly, the names restored to the record, and the two of them staying in a town that no longer belongs to either of them — a harbor, not a victory.
about_author: A. M. Underhill is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloging seized municipal records from contested border towns. They write historical fiction about the paperwork of atrocity and the people who refuse to let it stay filed.

chapters.title: The Weight of Minutes
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Summoned to the observatory to repair the master clock, Lior navigates the town's careful social silences — who may speak to whom, which names are not said. Inside the clock's case they find a hidden compartment and a ledger of erased names. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into dread as Lior recognizes a name they were taught never to speak — their mother's.

chapters.title: Requisition
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The imperial army occupies Vellmark; the observatory becomes a signals station and the town archive is sealed 'for inventory.' Lior hides the ledger inside a broken regulator clock and is conscripted to keep the station's timepieces running. Emotional beat: the old survival skill of silence now feels like complicity, and Lior resents the clock they once loved.

chapters.title: The Inventory Officer
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Captain Ilse Brandt, tasked with cataloging the observatory's instruments, notices the regulator's weight is wrong and a case freshly resealed. She says nothing — yet. Emotional beat: professional pride at war with a growing suspicion that her orders serve erasure, not order; she begins reading the town's seized records at night.

chapters.title: What the Magistrates Kept
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior seeks out old tobacconist Marta Vey, the only living name in the ledger's margins, and learns how the magistrates' purges were carried out — and how the clockmaker master, Lior's teacher, helped hide the record. Emotional beat: grief braided with fury; Lior understands the ledger was left for someone to find, and that they were meant to be that someone.

chapters.title: Armistice Weather
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Peace talks stall in the capital; rumors arrive that the army will burn the town archives before withdrawal to leave 'no disputed evidence.' Ilse finds a page of the ledger in a seized file and confronts the implication: her own regiment signed the deportation order for the Okafor family. Emotional beat: vertigo — her duty and her conscience pull in opposite directions for the first time.

chapters.title: A Bargain in the Clock Room
chapters.summary: Lior and Ilse's alternating POV. Ilse corners Lior about the hidden ledger; instead of arrest, an uneasy alliance forms — she can move through army channels, Lior knows the town's hiding places. Emotional beat: wary, electric trust between two people trained by opposing systems not to trust; the first time either speaks an erased name aloud to the other.

chapters.title: The Historian's Draft
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A victors' historian arrives to write the official account and interviews townsfolk, recording a version with no deportations at all. Lior watches neighbors, terrified, confirm the lie. Emotional beat: despair and clarity — the ledger is worthless unless it reaches the provisional assembly before the armistice is signed, which may be days away.

chapters.title: The Burn Order
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. The order comes down: destroy all seized records at dawn. Ilse falsifies the inventory to buy hours, knowing it ends her career and possibly her life. She and Lior plan the harbor route — the ledger sealed inside a chronometer crate bound for a neutral merchant ship. Emotional beat: cold resolve; love acknowledged in the space of a single look, neither daring to name it.

chapters.title: The Harbor at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The night run: checkpoints, a betrayed signal from a frightened neighbor, and Ilse taking a bullet in the shoulder holding the pier while Lior gets the crate aboard. The ship casts off as soldiers reach the quay. Emotional beat: the climax — terror, sacrifice, and the strange calm of a clockmaker's hands doing exact work while everything else burns.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: Lior and Ilse's alternating POV. The armistice is signed without the ledger, but the provisional assembly convenes anyway, and the names are read aloud over three days while the town stands in the rain to hear them. Ilse, stripped of commission, stays; Lior repairs the master clock and leaves the compartment empty, the record now living in public memory. Emotional beat: not triumph but restoration — a harbor built from truth, and two people choosing to remain in it.
